title: Can You Trust AI Citations? Catch Bad References in 3 Steps
description: An official link can be real while the claim beside it is wrong. Follow a clearly labeled teaching example: open the link, compare the original wording, read the context, and correct the answer. The source was opened on September 27, 2026. Official pages may change; check them again before relying on a citation.

ci001.text: This answer links to an official page, but its conclusion says the opposite.

ci002.text: If you only check for a link, you might pass the mistake along.

ci003.text: Let us break it down in three steps, then fix the answer.

ci004.text: First, this on-screen answer was deliberately written wrong for teaching.

ci005.text: It is not output from any real model.

ci006.text: False claim: the official guide says citations replace human fact-checking.

ci007.text: It even includes a real link to an official document.

ci008.text: This error is easy to miss because the URL really exists.

ci009.text: An official domain can make the adjacent claim feel true.

ci010.text: But a working link only proves there is a page.

ci011.text: It does not prove that page supports this conclusion.

ci080.text: The source link may point to the wrong page, or the page may be overinterpreted.

ci081.text: Worse, the information may have been right only in an older version.

ci082.text: So checking is more than picking a trustworthy-looking URL.

ci083.text: Match each specific claim to specific words in the source.

ci012.text: The three-step check asks three questions.

ci013.text: First, does the link really lead to the original source?

ci014.text: Second, which claim does the original text actually support?

ci015.text: Third, do the context or date change the meaning?

ci116.text: You may not have time to check a long list of sources.

ci031.text: The first might be right. It does not make the second right too.

ci088.text: A long answer often bundles many claims together.

ci089.text: Split them into sentences to see which have evidence.

ci090.text: For each, mark supported, contradicted, or not found.

ci091.text: Not found may mean the citation is wrong, not that you read too slowly.

ci124.text: A small citation at the end can make the whole paragraph look sourced.

ci128.text: A sourced answer is easier to check than one with no clues.

ci129.text: But you still need to open, read, and compare that source.

ci130.text: A citation is a signpost to possible evidence.

ci131.text: A signpost is not the evidence itself, and it is no guarantee.

ci037.text: The left-hand citation cannot certify the right-hand claim.

ci044.text: Step three: read the limits the source gives its own methods.

ci045.text: This document says these methods can reduce errors.

ci100.text: Before making a quote card, do not stop at one sentence.

ci101.text: The previous line may explain when it applies.

ci103.text: Cutting those conditions can mislead, even with a perfect quote.

ci136.text: A useful trick is to notice how strong the source's wording is.

ci052.text: The source's date also affects the answer.

ci053.text: An old article may have been right then but superseded now.

ci104.text: A credible source must also be relevant to the present.

ci105.text: An old article may explain the past without guiding today's choice.
